The district library in Bhilwara closed at seven, and Indu came every afternoon to prepare for the bank exam. The problem was Minakshi, her best friend, who worked at the cloth shop across the road. Around four, Minakshi would appear at the window, waving a steel tumbler. "Chai, Indu! Five minutes!" Five minutes always became an hour.
So on Sunday Indu wrote on the inside cover of her reasoning book: If Minakshi calls before six, I say, "Six o'clock at the chai stall."
On Monday, at four sharp, the tumbler waved. Indu's legs wanted to get up. She looked at the cover and walked to the window instead. "Six o'clock at the chai stall. Keep my cup hot."
Minakshi pulled a face and then laughed. Indu went back to puzzles. At six, the chai was waiting.

qa.a: She worked at the cloth shop across the road.

qa.a: Minakshi pulls a face at first, a bit disappointed, but then laughs and waits with the chai at six.

Lucia had lost three study afternoons in a row at the university library in Madrid. Each time her flatmate Jin texted, "Terrace? Sun's out," she'd pack up "for one coffee" and not come back.
On Thursday morning, over toast, she told Jin her plan. "If you text me before six, I'm going to write back 'Six, terrace.' Not now. Six."
Jin raised an eyebrow. "You're scheduling me?"
"I'm scheduling me."
At half past three the text came: "Terrace? It's glorious." Lucia's thumb hovered. The sun through the window looked very good. She typed exactly what she'd planned: "Six, terrace." Then she turned the phone face down.
At six she walked out with two chapters of statistics done. Jin had saved her a chair in the sun.

qa.a: She had lost three study afternoons in a row.

3 February
Healthier this year. That's what I wrote on 1 January in big letters on the first page of this diary. I, Indu, twenty-four, was going to be a new person.
Let's see. Week one I walked twice in the morning. Week two it was cold. Week three there was the audit, and Darshan kept bringing samosas to the office at four, and I kept eating them. By week four I had forgotten the resolution existed until I opened this diary today.
Healthier how? When? I never wrote any of that. Every morning I woke up and decided depending on how I felt, and most mornings I felt sleepy.
It's annoying that the page still looks so confident. I feel a bit silly. I think "healthier" needs a time and a place, or it's just a nice word.

Vinita's back had started aching from nine hours at the office desk in Salt Lake. Every Sunday she promised herself to stretch every day, and every day she forgot until she was already in bed.
Then her flatmate Leela, a physiotherapy student, said something over dinner. "Don't decide to stretch. Decide what comes before it. What do you do every night, no matter what?"
"Brush my teeth."

Three weeks later, Leela found her stretching at midnight after a wedding, still in her party clothes.

Vasudha's science-fair project on seed germination was due on Friday, and she had known about it for a month. Every evening she opened the folder, looked at the blank title page and closed it. If it turned out badly, everyone in Class 10 would see it on the board, with her name in big letters.
On Wednesday night she finally started. Then the power went off across the street, the inverter beeped and died, and the laptop she shared with her brother Yusuf had eleven percent battery. The seeds she had soaked were only a day old, not two weeks.
By candlelight, she drew sprouts she had never grown and wrote a conclusion she could not prove.
Yusuf, reading his comic with a torch, said, "Why didn't you start last month?"
Vasudha didn't answer. The honest reason was that starting would have meant being judged sooner.

qa.q: How much battery did the shared laptop have when the power went off?
qa.a: It had eleven percent battery.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha keep closing the folder for a month?
qa.a: She felt anxious that a bad result would be seen by the whole class with her name on it, so delaying protected her from being judged.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Vasudha try next time?
qa.a: Delaying left no time for the seeds to grow and no margin for the power cut; next time she could start with one small step early, like soaking the seeds, before worrying about the result.

qa.q: How does Yusuf see Vasudha's situation?
qa.a: Yusuf sees it simply as poor timing and asks why she didn't start earlier, not knowing the fear of judgement behind the delay.

grounding: It shows a teenager putting off a project because a poor result would expose her, which protects her self-image but makes the final work worse.

passage:
Ganga's school film club was screening every Class 11 short film in the auditorium, with parents invited. Her script had been ready in her head for weeks. Her camera, borrowed from her aunt, sat in its case.
"When are we shooting?" her friend Yamini asked on Monday. "I'm free all week to act."
"Soon. I'm still thinking."
She kept thinking. Thinking was safe. Nobody could call a film in your head clumsy.
On the Sunday before the screening, she finally called Yamini. They shot everything in one afternoon, in bad light, with the neighbour's pressure cooker whistling through every scene. There was no time to reshoot.
In the auditorium, the audience laughed at the wrong places. Ganga sank low in her seat. The film everyone saw really was clumsy, just as she had feared.

qa.q: When did Ganga finally call Yamini to shoot?
qa.a: Ganga called Yamini on the Sunday before the screening.

qa.q: Why did Ganga keep saying she was still thinking?
qa.a: She felt afraid that a real film would be judged as clumsy, while a film in her head could not fail, so delaying felt safe.

qa.q: What could Ganga have done differently?
qa.a: She could have shot a rough first version early in the week with Yamini, so there was time to fix the light and sound before anyone saw it.

qa.q: What is it like for Yamini to wait all week?
qa.a: Yamini, who was free to act all week, may feel frustrated and let down to end up rushing through one afternoon in bad light.

grounding: It shows a teenager delaying her film because a poor result might reveal weakness, which protects her self-image but makes the final film worse.

It was 2 a.m. in the architecture studio at the hostel, and Harsha was humming. Jury was at nine. His model of a riverside library was half cardboard, half imagination.
"I work best like this," he told his roommate Alka, who had finished her model three days earlier and had come only to help. "Pressure makes me brilliant."
The rush was real. His hands flew, his eyes were bright, he had drunk three cups of coffee. At four, he burned his finger on the glue gun and didn't stop. At six, he realised the staircase didn't reach the second floor.
Alka held the roof while it dried. "You said that last semester too," she said. "Remember the jury comment? 'Promising idea, rushed finish'?"
Harsha laughed, a little too loudly. His hands were shaking now, and not only from the coffee.

qa.q: What was Harsha's model of?
qa.a: It was a model of a riverside library.

qa.q: Why does Harsha believe the last-night rush suits him?
qa.a: He feels excited and alive under pressure, with his hands flying and eyes bright, so the panic feels like energy and brilliance.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could help next time?
qa.a: He burned his finger, the staircase didn't reach the second floor and last semester's jury called it rushed; next time he could set a false deadline two days early with Alka checking in.

qa.q: How might Alka feel about helping Harsha at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: Alka seems caring but tired and a little worried, reminding him gently that the same pattern hurt him last semester.

grounding: It shows a student who believes he works best under pressure leaving his model to the last night, where the rush gives energy but costs quality and health.

Subject: Survived (barely)
Hi Kiran,
Submitted the sociology term paper at 8:57 this morning. Deadline was 9. I started it at 10 last night. Yes, again.
You know my theory: I'm a pressure person. Give me three weeks and I do nothing; give me eleven hours and I'm a machine. And honestly, around 2 a.m. I felt amazing. Heart racing, ideas pouring out, typing like a pianist.
But I read it again after submitting, and oh no. Two paragraphs say the same thing. I cited a book I never actually opened. The conclusion just stops. And I have a pounding headache and my eyes feel like sandpaper.
Maybe the machine only feels fast from the inside.
Coffee at four? You can tell me "I told you so" in person. I've earned it.
Anjali

"You want to know how I do my assignments? Okay, Tejas, I'll tell you, but don't copy me. I'm Tanuja, and I'm famous in our batch for one thing: the all-nighter.
It's not that I'm lazy. I genuinely believe I think better when the clock is screaming. When there's a week left, my brain is mush. When there are six hours left, it's like a switch flips. I get this rush, almost like joy. Music loud, snacks everywhere, I'm unstoppable.
Last month, though. The economics project. I started at eleven, and at four in the morning I realised my data file was the wrong year. No time to fix it. I submitted anyway. Got a C. And I was sick for two days after, just wrecked.
So yes, the rush is real. So is what it costs. I'm trying to believe both at once."

"Mahima, the application closes Friday." Seema put down her chai. "Did you send it?"
"Which one?"
"Any one! The master's, the bank job, the fellowship. You had three tabs open in June."
"I still have them open."
"It's September."
"I know." Mahima picked at the edge of the table. "What if I pick the master's and it's the wrong field? That's two years. What if I take the bank job and get stuck forever? What if the fellowship is a waste?"
"So you've picked none."
"I haven't picked anything yet. I'm still deciding."
"Didi, not deciding is also deciding. The fellowship closed last week."
Mahima went quiet. She hadn't even noticed.
"Let's sit tonight and write down what each one gives you," Seema said. "Just tonight."

qa.q: How many options did Mahima have open in June?
qa.a: She had three tabs open: the master's, the bank job and the fellowship.

qa.q: Why does Mahima keep putting off the applications?
qa.a: She feels anxious that every option is risky and permanent, so not choosing feels safer than choosing wrong.

qa.q: What does Seema suggest, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: Seema suggests sitting together that night to write down what each option offers, which turns an overwhelming choice into a small, concrete task.

qa.q: How does Seema see Mahima's delay?
qa.a: Seema sees that the delay is already making choices for Mahima, since the fellowship closed while Mahima was still deciding.

grounding: It shows a graduate delaying every application because each option feels risky and irreversible, until not choosing becomes a choice by default.

Looking back at last year, the thing I notice is how busy I felt doing nothing. I'm Eshaan. After my BCom results, I had three paths: an MBA entrance, a job at my uncle's firm, or a year teaching with a rural fellowship.
Each one felt like a door that would lock behind me. The MBA felt too expensive to get wrong. The firm felt like forever. The fellowship felt like falling behind.
So I made lists. Then more lists. My friend Nilesh applied to two places in October and started one in January. I kept telling him I was still researching.
In March I looked up. The MBA registration had closed. The fellowship had filled. The firm had hired someone else.
I had been so scared of choosing the wrong door that I let every door close. Not deciding felt safe. It turned out to be a decision too.

qa.a: Nilesh applied to two places in October.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel about each of the three paths?
qa.a: Eshaan felt anxious and trapped, as if each one was a door that would lock behind, so choosing seemed dangerous.

qa.q: What could Eshaan have done differently in the autumn?
qa.a: Eshaan could have set a date to decide and applied to at least one path, remembering that most choices can be changed later.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have seen Eshaan's constant research?
qa.a: Nilesh, who applied and started somewhere, might have felt worried and puzzled watching a friend keep researching while deadlines passed.

Career counsellor's note, placement cell — Avni
Kamal, final-year engineering graduate. Fourth session.
He arrived with the same printed list as in July: two job offers to accept or decline, and a master's form. Both offers expire this month. He has not replied to either.
When I asked him to pick one to talk about, he said, "What if I choose the service company and it kills my career? What if I choose the start-up and it shuts down?" He rubbed his forehead and looked exhausted.
I pointed out that one offer's reply date is Thursday, and that if he does nothing, the company will choose for him.
He was quiet for a while. Then he said, "So waiting isn't neutral."
Next steps: we listed three things he cares about most. He will score each offer against them by Tuesday, and we meet Wednesday to decide.

qa.q: When is one offer's reply date?
qa.a: One offer's reply date is Thursday.

qa.q: What does Kamal's rubbing his forehead and looking exhausted suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels anxious and worn out, stuck because every option feels risky and permanent.

qa.q: How does the counsellor help Kamal move forward?
qa.a: The counsellor points out that waiting lets the company decide, then has Kamal score the offers against three things he cares about by Tuesday, with a meeting Wednesday.

qa.q: How might the start-up see Kamal's silence?
qa.a: The start-up may read his lack of reply as lost interest and move on, which is how not choosing becomes a choice by default.

grounding: It shows, through a counsellor's note, a graduate delaying his reply because every option feels risky and irreversible, until waiting becomes a choice by default.

Peer mentor's log, first-year hostel block — Vaibhav
Week 6. Hansa, my mentee from the English batch, told me on Monday she would start the literature essay "tomorrow for sure." She said the same thing last Monday and the Monday before.
Each time she says it, she looks a little more tired. Today she admitted she hadn't slept well because she kept thinking about the essay. "I'm just the kind of person who can't start," she said. That worried me more than the essay.
I didn't lecture. I asked if she'd sit with me in the common room for twenty minutes, phones away, and do only the easiest bit, the title and three quotes she liked.
She agreed, a bit reluctantly. After twenty minutes she had the title, four quotes and one rough sentence. She laughed and said, "That's more than two weeks."
We'll do the same on Thursday.

qa.q: What did Hansa have after twenty minutes?
qa.a: She had the title, four quotes and one rough sentence.

qa.q: What worried Vaibhav most about Hansa, and why?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt most worried when Hansa said she was "just the kind of person who can't start", because each failed tomorrow was making her feel worse about herself.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav's offer work better than a lecture?
qa.a: Sitting together for only twenty minutes on the easiest bit made starting small and less lonely, which broke the cycle of promises.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel after the twenty minutes?
qa.a: Hansa felt relieved and a little surprised, laughing that she had done more in twenty minutes than in two weeks.

grounding: It shows, through a peer mentor's log, a friend noticing a classmate keep promising to start tomorrow and offering twenty minutes together on the easiest piece.

14 October, night
Deepika said it again today at lunch: "I'll start the lab report tomorrow, pakka." I, Lakshmi, have heard "pakka" from her four times now.
The strange part is that she looks worse each time. Today she barely touched her rajma. She said, "I'm so useless, I don't know what's wrong with me." I didn't know what to say, and I felt awful, because I've done this too, with my thesis outline last year.
So after dinner I knocked on her door and said, "Twenty minutes. I'll sit here with my own notes. You just do the easiest part."
She chose the aim and the list of apparatus. Took her ten minutes. Then she kept going for another half hour, and I pretended to read.
When I left she said thank you twice. Tomorrow, same time. Pakka.

qa.q: How many times has Lakshmi heard Deepika say "pakka"?
qa.a: Lakshmi has heard it four times now.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when Deepika called herself useless?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt awful and unsure what to say, partly because Lakshmi had done the same thing with a thesis outline last year.

qa.q: What made Lakshmi's offer helpful?
qa.a: Offering to sit nearby for twenty minutes and start with the easiest part made beginning feel small and supported, which got Deepika going.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel at the end of the evening?
qa.a: Deepika probably feels relieved and grateful, saying thank you twice after finally making real progress.

grounding: It shows a friend who watches a classmate promise to start tomorrow again and again, feeling worse each time, and offers twenty minutes together on the easiest piece.
